metadata.title: Move the Part That Isn't Blocked.
metadata.topic: Humanitarians AI website restructure — Week 4: navigation and footer link cleanup carried out with the developer, and a four-part design-to-development collaboration framework
metadata.purpose: Week 4 of 4 project-status reel for the Humanitarians AI UX/UI restructure
metadata.skill: explainer (custom vox-style build — same Manim-for-every-beat approach as Weeks 1-3)

metadata.notes: IMPORTANT STATUS POINT, verified on the live site 2026-09-06: the link cleanup is DECIDED and SPECIFIED but NOT YET DEPLOYED. The homepage still carries all 11 Projects-column links and all five flagged names, and the footer still measures 33 column links / 39 anchors — identical to the Weeks 2 and 3 measurements. B08 states this explicitly so no viewer can open the site and catch the video overclaiming. The before/after arithmetic in B06 is therefore stated as current vs agreed, not current vs live.
metadata.shorts_note: 9:16 derives from this same beat_sheet via ./art shorts. Verify short/manim/ actually fills — on Week 1 that step scaffolded the folder and rendered nothing.

beats.narration_text: Hello, I am Muskan Agrawal, and this video is a summary of Week Four of the Humanitarians AI website restructure: a navigation cleanup done directly with the developer, and a working agreement for how design and development hand work to each other.
beats.new_visual_element: Cold open — presenter card

beats.narration_text: First, an honest status. The stakeholder meeting prepared in Week Three has not happened yet. The clarity it is meant to produce, on audience priority, messaging and success metrics, is still pending. Waiting for it would have cost a week.
beats.new_visual_element: Status card — what is still pending

beats.narration_text: So the week moved the part that was not blocked. Not everything in a restructure depends on knowing the audience. Removing links to things that do not exist does not.
beats.new_visual_element: Black card — MOVE THE PART THAT ISN'T BLOCKED

beats.narration_text: Working with the developer, the Week Two link audit stopped being a report and became a working document. We went through every navigation and footer link together and asked one question of each: is there a defined project behind this.
beats.new_visual_element: Card — the audit becomes a working document

beats.narration_text: The Projects column is where the answer was most often no. Eleven links today. Five of them point at names a first time visitor cannot decode and that have no built out concept behind them: Dewey, Madison, Medhavy, Mycroft, Popper.
beats.new_visual_element: Footer screenshot, Projects column boxed, count chips

shot.hold_reason: Projects-column box measured from 06_footer.jpg pixels in Week 2 — see SHOTLIST.md

beats.narration_text: Those five are the same names the Week One audit flagged, and the same ones Week Three counted as bare proper nouns. Three videos found them. This week they were actually scoped for removal, with the developer in the room.
beats.new_visual_element: The five names, struck from the list row by row

beats.narration_text: The arithmetic is small and real. The Projects column goes from eleven links to six. The footer's column links go from thirty three to twenty eight. Of the six bare proper nouns counted in Week Three, one remains. No redesign required.
beats.new_visual_element: Three before/after counters

beats.narration_text: This is the cheapest improvement in the entire project. No new layout, no new type, no new colour. Eleven links become six, and a first time visitor stops meeting five dead ends dressed as projects.
beats.new_visual_element: White card — the cheapest improvement

beats.narration_text: To be precise about status: this is decided and specified, not yet deployed. Measured on the live site today, the old links are still there. The decision is made; shipping it is the developer's next task.
beats.new_visual_element: Status card — decided, specified, not yet deployed

beats.narration_text: With the navigation scoped to real content, the rest of the week went somewhere less visible and more useful: agreeing how design and development would actually work together before any visuals started.
beats.new_visual_element: Turn card — process before pixels

beats.narration_text: Most handoff friction is not a disagreement about design. It is a disagreement about what a finished handoff looks like, discovered halfway through.
beats.new_visual_element: Black card — where handoff friction actually comes from

beats.narration_text: So the question went to the developer first. Would she rather inspect components, spacing and style values directly in Figma dev mode, or receive a written handoff with specs, component states and requirements documented before implementation begins. Her answer sets the format.
beats.new_visual_element: Two-option comparison — dev mode inspection vs documented handoff

beats.narration_text: Out of that conversation, a four part collaboration framework. One: a shared component library in Figma that mirrors the site's actual coded components, so navigation elements are not redesigned from a blank page each time. Two: dev mode access with clean, structured layer naming.
beats.new_visual_element: Framework parts one and two

beats.narration_text: The component library is the part that compounds. If the file mirrors what is actually coded, every later screen starts from real components instead of a redrawing of them, and the gap between design and build stops widening.
beats.new_visual_element: Card — why the shared library compounds

beats.narration_text: Three: a short written spec for interaction states. Hover, focus, active, and the mobile collapsed state for the navigation. Four: agreed breakpoint definitions, so the navigation behaves predictably across mobile, tablet and desktop instead of being decided twice.
beats.new_visual_element: Framework parts three and four

beats.narration_text: Interaction states are the classic gap. A design file shows one state. A browser has to show four. Whatever is not specified gets invented at build time, and then argued about at review.
beats.new_visual_element: Four interaction states, drawn as four chips

beats.narration_text: The week closed with a working session on technical feasibility and a staged rollout, and a phase by phase roadmap written down, so implementation has an order rather than a wish list.
beats.new_visual_element: Staged rollout — phases drawn in order

beats.narration_text: Four weeks. An audit, a specification, a set of questions, and a working agreement. The site does not look different yet. What changed is that every decision behind the rebuild is now written down, measured, or agreed with someone.
beats.new_visual_element: The four-week arc, complete

beats.narration_text: Still open: the stakeholder meeting, and the answers it owes on audience and messaging. That is what the navigation and hero rebuild waits on now.
beats.new_visual_element: Card — what remains open

beats.narration_text: Humanitarians dot A I restructure. Week four of four.
beats.new_visual_element: End card
